title: NIST AI 600-1 (Generative AI Profile) to the EU AI Act (amended)

useCase.intendedUsers: Lead auditors and reviewers of generative AI systems on engagements that use the AI Act as criteria.
useCase.purpose: Show which AI Act obligations bear on the twelve generative AI risks of NIST AI 600-1, so that evidence on the obligations can be read against the risks.

conceptTypes.source: Generative AI risk areas (NIST AI 600-1 section 2)

useCase.assumptions: A risk area is read as the outcome that the risk is identified and managed. Relationships compare subject matter, not how an organisation implements either side. Each entry is single-source, so it can be read in both directions. No inference may be drawn from outcomes or requirements that are not mapped. Every entry is intersects_with: a NIST outcome and the other requirement only overlap, so a full result on one side is never shown as full on the other. The NIST side was read against section 2 of NIST AI 600-1 (checked 2026-11-13). The AI Act side follows the eu-ai-act framework data (rule pack 2026.11.2), pending qualified legal review (D-02); the links were not legally reviewed.

entries.justification: Confabulation is a failure of accuracy; managing it overlaps with the appropriate accuracy of Art. 15(1), which applies to high-risk systems and sets no generative-specific measure.
Measuring confabulation rates overlaps with declaring accuracy metrics under Art. 15(3); a declared metric need not address confabulation.

Managing data privacy risk overlaps with the safeguards of Art. 4a for special categories of personal data used for bias detection; most privacy duties sit in data protection law, outside this framework.
Managing harmful bias overlaps with examining data for possible biases under Art. 10(2)(f); homogenisation of outputs is outside Art. 10.
Managing harmful bias overlaps with measures to detect, prevent and mitigate biases under Art. 10(2)(g).
The human-AI configuration risk includes automation bias and over-reliance, which overlap with keeping overseers aware of automation bias under Art. 14(4)(b).
Telling people that they interact with an AI system under Art. 50(1) addresses part of the anthropomorphising risk of the human-AI configuration risk, not its other aspects.

Machine-readable marking and detectability of synthetic outputs under Art. 50(2) address part of the information integrity risk; the risk also covers content that does not distinguish fact from opinion.
Disclosing deep fakes under Art. 50(4) addresses part of the information integrity risk for image, audio and video content.
Disclosing AI-generated text published on matters of public interest under Art. 50(4) addresses a narrow part of the information integrity risk.

The information security risk includes attacks on training data and model weights, which overlap with the AI-specific cybersecurity of Art. 15(5); lowered barriers to offensive cyber capabilities are outside it.
The value chain risk includes improperly obtained data, which overlaps with recording data collection processes and origin under Art. 10(2)(b).

notes: Every risk area was examined. CBRN information (2.1), dangerous, violent or hateful content (2.3), environmental impacts (2.5), intellectual property (2.10) and obscene, degrading or abusive content (2.11) have no entry: the obligations that bear on them (for example the duties of providers of general-purpose AI models in Art. 53 and 55) are not in the eu-ai-act framework data, so no AI Act evidence of this platform reaches them. Not an official NIST crosswalk.
